analysis.one_liner: Restores federal climate and air-pollution rules the Trump administration repealed, froze, or proposed weakening.
analysis.headline: The bill won 21 senators' backing but never received a committee hearing or vote; it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cancel Executive Order 13783 and reinstate a series of Obama-era climate rules that the Trump administration repealed, delayed, or replaced: the Clean Power Plan's limits on power-plant carbon emissions, federal limits on methane waste from oil and gas drilling on public lands, limits on landfill emissions, and energy-efficiency rules for light bulbs. It would also block several proposed rollbacks, including weaker fuel-economy standards, and restore California's authority to set stricter vehicle emission standards. It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who breathes outdoor air: the bill would restore limits on carbon pollution from power plants, methane waste and pollution from oil and gas operations on public land, emissions from landfills, and weaker tailpipe standards, and it would let California keep enforcing stricter vehicle emissions. Cleaner air and slower growth in greenhouse gases reduce respiratory illness, especially in communities near power plants, wells, highways, and landfills.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living near power plants, wells, highways

how_it_helps.text: Nullifies the repeal of the Clean Power Plan and its replacement emission guidelines, putting limits on greenhouse gas emissions from existing power plants back in effect [S2][S3]
Restores the Bureau of Land Management rule restricting methane waste from oil and gas production on federal lands, which had been delayed and suspended [S2][S3]
Blocks finalization of the proposed SAFE vehicle rules, which would have weakened fuel-economy and emissions standards for cars and light trucks through model year 2026 [S2][S3]
Nullifies any rescission of California's Clean Air Act waiver and bars the EPA from rescinding it again, preserving stricter state-level vehicle emission standards that other states follow [S2][S3]

Restores EPA rules limiting emissions from municipal solid waste landfills and DOE energy-efficiency rules for lamps, and cancels Executive Order 13783, which directed agencies to review and roll back climate regulations [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers on public lands, coal-fired power plants, and vehicle manufacturers would bear the compliance costs of the restored standards, which could be passed to consumers in the form of energy prices and vehicle costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, gas, coal, and auto companies

drawbacks.text: Restoring the Clean Power Plan and methane rules imposes compliance costs on power plants and drillers, and some of those costs flow through to electricity and fuel prices for households [S2][S3]

The bill re-instates specific prior rules by name with no reopening of the record, so the standards are locked in as written in 2015-2018 rather than updated through the normal regulatory process [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and climate benefits of restored air-pollution limits are broad and shared, while the costs fall on a concentrated set of energy and manufacturing firms and, partly, on consumers. The main design weakness is that the bill reinstates old rules verbatim instead of allowing agencies to update them, trading regulatory flexibility for certainty against further rollbacks.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Michael Bennet introduced the bill on September 18, 2019, with 21 Democratic and independent senators signed on as original sponsors or cosponsors [S1][S4]
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources that same day; that was the bill's last action [S5]
The bill died in committee when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and no version of it was ever debated or voted on in either chamber [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers, coal-fired utilities, and automakers stayed under the weaker standards because the restored rules never took effect, and the proposed rollbacks went forward unchallenged by this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil, gas, coal, and auto interests

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers on public lands
industries.note: The bill restores the BLM methane-waste rule the industry had gotten suspended and blocks the weaker EPA emission standards for the oil and gas sector, raising drilling compliance costs. Methane leaks waste gas the public owns and worsen air quality near drilling operations.
The bill nullifies the repeal of the Clean Power Plan, putting carbon limits on existing power plants back in effect. Plants that emit the most would face the largest costs.

The bill blocks the SAFE vehicle rules that would have loosened fuel-economy and tailpipe standards through 2026, and preserves California's stricter standards. Consumers would pay somewhat more per vehicle but save on fuel over its life.
The bill reinstates EPA emission guidelines for municipal solid waste landfills that had been weakened, requiring emissions controls at some facilities.

The bill restores the DOE general service lamp definition and blocks the withdrawal of efficiency standards for incandescent lamps, keeping stricter energy-efficiency requirements in place for bulbs sold in the U.S.
